title: Call on Me
hook: your Lord said, call on Me and I will answer (40:60)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ghafir, the surah of the believer in Pharaoh's house, and your line was one voice inside. Did you get to be the calm question in a room? Day five hundred sixty-three.

There's a kind of person who'd rather drive in circles for half an hour than stop and ask for directions. Or carry a heavy couch up three flights alone rather than text a neighbor. Or sit with a problem for months rather than say the words, I need help. It's not that they can't ask. Something in them won't. Back on day one hundred thirty, this path met du'a, the open, anytime prayer of asking. Today's verse comes back to it from the other side: what it says about the person who won't ask.

Surah Ghafir, verse sixty. Pickthall: "And your Lord hath said: Pray unto me and I will hear your prayer. Lo! those who scorn My service, they will enter hell, disgraced." Hear the two halves together. The first is an invitation and a promise: ud'uni, call on Me, astajib lakum, I will answer you. The second is a warning, and here's the surprise: it isn't aimed at people who ask for the wrong things. It's aimed at those too proud. The Arabic is yastakbiruna, from kibr, the same pride the Qur'an names when Iblis refused to bow. Too proud for what? 'an 'ibadati, for My worship. The verse begins with asking and ends with worship, as if they were the same thing. And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ read it that way. In Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, he says du'a is worship, and recites this very verse. So, in this verse, not asking isn't a sign of strength. It can be pride. There's a hadith in al-Tirmidhi that puts it sharply: whoever doesn't ask Allah, Allah is displeased with him. People tire of being asked. In this hadith, it's the not-asking that displeases. When someone asks, they admit they need, and the hadith counts that asking as worship. So the verse turns the couch-carrying instinct upside down. In it, asking isn't weakness to be avoided. It's the invitation.

The practice: make a du'a, trusting the answer. Sit, and notice one thing you've been carrying alone, too proud or too tired to ask for help with. If you pray, ask Allah for it now, plainly, in your own words, and let go of how the answer will come. If you don't pray, simply name the need out loud, to yourself, and think of one person you could ask. Either way, sit with the asking done. The bell holds the time.
Ud'uni, call on Me, Ghafir sixty's invitation and promise, paired with a warning for those too proud to ask. Today's word.
Your line: call, and be answered. Today, ask for one thing you'd normally carry alone, from God if you pray, and from one person either way. Day five hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims make du'a at any time and in any language, often raising their hands, and especially after prayers, in the last third of the night, and between the call to prayer and its start.

fork.setup: you've carried a problem alone for months. you could ask God, and others, for help. what does 40:60 say about not asking?
options: it's a sign of strong faith.
it can be a kind of pride.
fork.reveal: the verse warns those too proud for His worship, and the Prophet read asking as worship itself.

original.note: Arabic: call on Me, I will answer you (40:60).

trapdoor: what you thought: if you need something, you can pray.
what it means: asking is worship, and refusing to ask can be pride.
what a scholar hears: 40:60 pairs ud'uni with 'an 'ibadati; the Prophet recites it after 'du'a is worship' (Abu Dawud 1479, Tirmidhi 2969); kibr links the refusal to Iblis's.
